speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SUMMER EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promised some months ago that I would make a statement on the experience with summer employment for students. Recently another question about this matter was asked in the House, and with this in mind I should like to report briefly on results last summer and to indicate some of the initiatives currently being followed by my department to assist students in finding jobs next summer.
Based on a survey carried out by my department last fall, some 323,000 students were able to find paying jobs last summer. I may say that the survey covered 39 postsecondary institutions-universities, colleges and technological	institutes-across the
country.
Of the roughly 400,000 students from postsecondary institutions, some 348,000 were in the summer employment market and of these 93 per cent found summer work. An estimated 323,000 of the 348,000 students who sought paid summer employment found jobs. Of these, 14 per cent worked for more than four months, 60 per cent for two to four months, 18 per cent for one to two months, and 8 per cent for less than a month.
This is generally a good result and encourages us to maintain and expand the program launched to assist student employment in the past summer. Of those who were not looking for jobs, nearly half continued their studies; another 25 per cent travelled, took time off or did unpaid volunteer work.
Half of those who found employment expressed satisfaction with the duration of their jobs. One-third would have liked two months more work and 11 per cent stated they would have worked more than two months.
Of the students working, 72 per cent were employed in industry and 14 per cent with provincial governments across Canada, while 7 per cent were granted employment with the federal government and a further 7 per cent with municipalities.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The federal government hired some 11,365 students, an increase of 26.8 per cent over the previous year. Students working for the federal governments earned $11,129,417 in salaries and wages. Seventy-five per cent of those hired were returning to post-secondary institutions. Students of post-secondary institutions in federal employment earned an average of $1,083, while high school students earned an average of $654.
Finally, plans are under way in my department, in co-operation with private and public organizations and provincial government departments, to complete plans and programs for the coming summer months. A national committee for student summer employment is functioning and includes representatives of the Association of Canadian Universities and Colleges, the University Career Planning Association, the Economic Council of Canada and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. Working through manpower centres both across the country and at the universities, as well as with federal and provincial departments of government, it is hoped that employment can be provided for the majority of students in order to obtain funds to finance their continued education.
In closing I would pay tribute to the energetic campaign being carried on by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce through its members, who have been working closely with my department to make the "Hire a Student" campaign a success next summer.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SUMMER EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS

Mr. Speaker, I received a copy of the minister's statement just as I took my seat. I should like to make a few comments on what the minister has said and about this problem.
There can be no question that a number of students had difficulty obtaining employment last summer, and presumably difficulty will be encountered again this summer. I suggest

this will result from the general employment conditions in the country and the policies of the government regarding employment, austerity programs and so on. These policies have increased unemployment substantially and have had an effect on students as well as others seeking work. On the basis of the present outlook we can expect quite a difficult summer in terms of students obtaining employment.
While the minister has said he has an advisory board and a program that is getting under way, I do not think anyone can stress too strongly the necessity for the minister and those with whom he is associated to understand fully the gravity of the situation and the implications for students who are not able to obtain work. Unfortunately we face a situation in which not only is employment becoming more difficult to obtain but also the number of students who need the extra money is increasing. Not only does the minister have to launch a considerably more vigor-' ous program than we have seen to date but the government of Canada in association with the provinces must take a very careful look to determine the over-all position of these students and the extent to which students are being forced to drop out or defer their education for financial reasons.
I am disappointed that rather than working with the provinces with a view to meeting this problem the government has indicated in the white paper on tax reform that it is going to subject bursaries to income tax. This can only serve to increase the difficulties. We all recognize that if a student cannot continue his studies at a particular time in life he or she may well suffer irreparable injury with the result, of course, that the nation also suffers.
While I welcome the minister's statement and his assurance that he is working on this very serious problem, quite frankly I see no indication that the government is prepared to grapple with student assistance by placing it in context with the over-all unemployment problem. I urge the minister and the Prime Minister to really take this matter seriously, particularly in view of the fact that their policies are designed to create unemployment and incidentally create additional difficulty for our students.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SUMMER EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too received the minister's statement a few minutes ago just as I entered the House. We in this party welcome the minister's statement of his intentions which I am 
sure are good. However, I believe we are in complete agreement that the statement does not go far enough. It barely scratches the surface.
The minister pointed out that 93 per cent of students seeking work found employment last summer, but he went on to say that about half of them were not satisfied with the employment they obtained. We must remember that many students who obtained employment last summer were remunerated at a rate which did not enable them to return to university. Several students from my province of Saskatchewan have written or spoken to me or to some of my colleagues pointing out that they just could not find employment last summer in the province of Saskatchewan which is suffering from some economic hardship. Something must be done immediately because this situation has handicapped many students and made it difficult for them to attend university. This is particularly so in the case of women who find that their salaries are lower and who do not wish to borrow huge sums of money in order to attend university.
We must remember that educated people are our main resource. Therefore I believe top priority should be given to this whole problem. The answer is not simply the finding of jobs. University education should be made available to everyone. If there is universal accessibility to education we will also have to provide more jobs for our working people.
I welcome the minister's statement but it by no means goes far enough toward solving the problem.

May I answer questions asked by the Leader of the Opposition on Tuesday with respect to lay-offs in the automobile industry? The two probing questions asked were, first, whether notice has been given in such instances and, second, whether the situation is worse in Canada than in the United States.
I have looked into this situation. To answer a distinction must be made between two types of lay-offs. One type is for restructuring. We have had two instances of that type, both in Chrysler Corporation. In each of these two instances notice was given to employees several weeks in advance.

It is a disappointment to me that the amendment I proposed was ruled out of order, but I hope the minister will take the necessary steps to ensure that a correction is made so that the provincial treasury branches can enjoy equal status with the other financial institutions which operate in the province and in the rest of the country.

Certainly, the profits that accrue from institutions such as provincial treasury branches go back into the provincial revenue, and in this way part of the load is taken off the public purse, which I think is most important in view of the country's present economic situation.
Much of the profit of our other banking institutions eventually finds its way outside the country. I am not debating the merits or otherwise of this situation, but I do say that it would be a gross discrimination and contrary to the public interest for the federal government not to extend the same privileges to provincial treasury branches as they do to private financial institutions especially when, as I said earlier, we have clear precedents for this type of guarantee.
There is one other important addition which could have been made to this biU and that is the inclusion of inventory and accounts receivable so that loans could be made on this basis as well as for business expansion. I think that small business across Canada is facing very serious problems and, indeed, in many eases is faced with the problem of whether it will be able to survive over the next period of years. This has come about, Mr. Speaker, in large part because of the increasing concentration of economic power within Canada. Thus, many small businesses find it difficult to compete with large corporations, large monopolies or even conglomerates, not only because of problems of competing in price but also because of problems in commanding adequate amounts of the resources necessary to enable small businesses to take advantage of the technological advances which would enable them to give their customers the type of service and product which is required.

As I pointed out earlier in the debate, one of the major purposes of the amendments before us is to extend the lending period under the legislation so that small business loans can continue to be made. The proposal is that the lending period be extended for a further 18 months to June 30, 1971 rather than for a three year period as has been the case in the past. This would bring the lending periods contemplated in all three acts into line as far as terminal dates are concerned.
This will enable the government to carry out a review of these three programs concurrently. Such a review would permit the government to examine the entire scope of the operation, the results of the program, and the question as to whether any changes ought to be made. This review will be carried out in a way which will enable us to look at one program in the light of the experience with the others in so far as this would seem relevant. I believe that many of the suggestions made by hon. members during this stage of the debate and previously are suggestions which ought to be considered in the course of this review. For example, the point raised by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey) and others with respect to including the Alberta treasury branches under the terms of the Small Businesses Loans Act is one which might be considered at that time. We should remember that the original objective of this legislation, together with its companion measures, was to facilitate by means of government guarantees a flow of credit for certain purposes by financial institutions to small business and certain other categories of enterprise. To include agencies such as the Alberta treasury branches as eligible to receive the federal government guarantee under this law and the two companion laws would raise a very broad question as to the eligibility of lending agencies of provincial governments, and, perhaps, in some cases, even of municipal governments. This, as I say, is a broad question which would extend beyond the matter of Alberta treasury branches, which, as hon. members have said, are playing a significant part in the financial life of the 21611-50
Canada Student Loans Act province of Alberta, and I think hon. members will agree we should want to give such a suggestion serious consideration. A good opportunity for carrying out such an examination would certainly be during the course of the review to which I have referred.
I also wish to say that while the terms of this legislation and the companion legislation do not authorize the government to order the financial institutions in question to make the type of loans contemplated, the guarantee loans administration of the Department of Finance is willing to investigate complaints of the type raised by the hon. member for Gan-der-Twillingate. If he, and other members of the House would like to bring to my personal attention complaints which have been brought to their notice by those who have sought loans under these acts I would be happy to have those complaints looked into and have reports made on them as soon as possible.
Let me in conclusion point out, as I did on another occasion when this subject was before the House, that though lending under the small businesses loans program never approached the volume reached under the Farm Improvement Loans Act it has, nevertheless, been a useful source of term financing for Canadian business. Since its inception some 20,000 small businesses have obtained financing amounting to almost $190 million under this program and the proposals in Bill C-9 will help ensure that credit facilities of this kind continue to be available to assist small businessmen in Canada through arrangements encouraged by the federal government.

I have a few comments to make at this stage, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the legislation
January 29, 1970

Canada Student Loans Act before us. It is an interesting piece of legislation. I do not know how widely this interest extends, since there do not appear to be many other speakers. Nevertheless, it is interesting to me.
This bill will broaden the sources of lending by the inclusion of trust and loan companies. Scholastic standards originally defined in the legislation now appear in another section and are left more or less to the provinces in terms of eligibility for loans. I notice, too, that a little hypocrisy has been removed from the bill. Landed immigrants no longer have to pledge that they plan to stay in Canada permanently before being accepted for a student loan. I think it would have been a simple matter for anyone to have got around this provision if they did not wish to be completely frank when making a declaration of this kind.
I notice there is now a provision in the bill fixing a semester maximum of $500 in connection with a student loan. This is perhaps in recognition of the fact that various postsecondary institutions in Canada are now embarking on newer kinds of school sessions. This may be all to the good. I am pleased that this legislation has recognized this fact. I am sorry that the student loans are continuing to be limited to full-time students. I submit it might be well worth while broadening this kind of assistance to include those who, for one reason or another, cannot attend an institution full-time but are nevertheless interested in upgrading their education during such time as they do have available. In this respect, I think Canada has been particularly remiss. We have failed to provide enough opportunities for people to gain extra education at times other than the normal dayschool time.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I think the trend today is changing. How often do we hear it said of a famous man, perhaps not so much in this country as in others, that he was originally a ditch digger who got his law degree at night school? I suggest that it would be useful indeed to broaden this legislation in this regard, and this is why I am a little critical of the provision of the bill that restricts the legislation to full-time students only. The basic loan provided under the legislation is increased to $115 million. It is to be applied on a sliding scale formula, and I should like to comment on this feature later.
The student loans legislation has been very popular if its popularity can be judged by the

number of people who have taken advantage of it. I have before me a press release by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) dated September 12, 1969 and I should like to quote the first paragraph. The press release is entitled "Canada Student Loans Plan" and reads:
The Honourable E. J. Benson, Minister of Finance, announced today that loans totalling $65,767,496 to 107,145 students were authorized under the Canada Student Loans Plan during the period of July 1, 1968 to June 30, 1969. In the previous year-
That is the year 1967-68.
-loans totalling $57,053,410 to 90,371 students were authorized.
This indicates two things to me. One is that I think people are showing a great and increasing interest in education. Secondly, I think it also indicates something that perhaps most members, are not quite so ready to talk about in this Parliament-I am, but there are some members who are reluctant-namely that if more students are required to borrow money to finance their education, it is because there are fewer opportunities for them to earn money by summer employment. I suggest it also indicates an economic down-turn which limits the opportunities for those students who have financed themselves in the past but cannot equally well do so today.
I suggest this is a matter into which we should look, because not only does it indicate an increasing interest on the part of young people to educate themselves, but it also indicates, or to be fair perhaps I should say it may indicate, a down-turn in the economy. As a result, in order to get their education they have to go into hock by taking a loan to be repaid over a period of nine and a half years at varying rates of interest. I do not know how the rest of the members of the House feel about this but I think this practice may well impose an extreme burden upon them. Certainly, the nine and a half years following my graduation from university were the most economically deprived of my life.

That is a substantial amount of money and shows that a substantial number of students have been assisted by this loan provision. But this is far in excess of the 10,000 student scholarships-I underline the word "scholarships"-that were part of a campaign pledge made by former Prime Minister, Lester B. Pearson.
But, Mr. Speaker, student loans are really but a half-way house, when you really get down to examining their rationale. Although they are necessary under our present system, they are definitely a crutch. Up to 80 per cent of the cost of secondary education today is paid by the government, either federal or provincial.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) made a statement to the House today on the efforts being made to increase employment opportunities for summer students. I think that since industry, the public and our institutions all benefit from education, not forgetting the benefit received by the students themselves, it would seem to me that it would only be logical to raise the other 20 per cent of the cost of education. We might then arrive at the point where those students who require summer employment in order to finance their education would not at the same time be competing against heads of families who are often marginally employed, in some cases putting them out of work, and this in spite of the fact that there is usually a seasonal upswing in summer employment opportunities. I think we should examine tuition costs from this point of view. I am not sure that this House, however, is the right place to look at the matter in view of the limits of federal jurisdiction in educational matters. Nevertheless, I feel the subject is worthy of mention.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to comment on the sliding scale that is being proposed in the legislation. This scale is based not on the number of young people in Canada between the ages of 18 and 24 but, instead, on the number of students presently enrolled in post-secondrary education who are between the ages of 18 and 24. The formula is based on what the condition is rather than on what the condition should be. The formula ignores the fact that in this age group of 18 to 24, 50 per cent of our students may have never completed high school. These people should be encouraged to complete their education assured that they will find a place in higher education. These dropouts are indicative of a waste of talent and an inefficient use of

Canada Student Loans Act human resources. Their talents should be developed to contribute to the development of this country.
I would also suggest to the House that one of the difficulties encountered in the provision of secondary education is that education is often not accessible to students with merit or scholastic ability but instead is provided only to those by affluent parents and to those students who live reasonably close to a university. I believe we should look more and more to the time when students attend university on the basis of ability, not on the basis of how much money their parents have. If necessary, the students should receive travel assistance. Today our university students represent a relatively small and affluent section of the population. We must do much more to see that university education is spread uniformly and fairly through the total population. Intelligence is not confined to any single economic class.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
That is the main emphasis I put on the remarks I made this afternoon. I feel the legislation is perhaps of assistance to many students. There will be an increasing number of students who wish to take advantage of this measure. They will not only wish to do so but will be forced to because there are no other alternative provisions to adequately fulfil the demands and needs of young Canadians for post secondary education.

It has been suggested that there are few opportunities today for Canadian students. Again, a main reason for the increase in the number of student loans is the fact that a great many more people are desirous of obtaining a university education. This is a favourable situation. My main aim, however, is to lend my support to the suggestion made by the capable chairman of our caucus committee, and other members, regarding the restriction being placed on students eligible for loans, in that they must be full-time students.
The Government of Canada has recognized that the provinces have to be given more flexibility in the determination of who should receive a loan. I suggest that this government should also permit the provinces to determine what constitutes a student rather than limiting this definition by the words "a full-time student", who must be in attendance during not less than one semester. This limitation is to be found in clause 1, subclause (3), paragraph (i). I am not a lawyer but I think that is the part. I cannot understand the need for this restriction or inflexibility.

First of all, the use of the word "semester" in a chancy thing because there are about 25 different definitions in various universities across the country. But on the main point, why should the student be a "full-time student"? In many areas, where salaries are low, teachers are without full qualifications and receive small wages, these people must obtain their education by attending evening classes or summer schools. They are not able to enrol as full-time students at universities.
Many thousands of teachers across Canada are not able to attend universities full time because they are married and have families which they must support. the setting of scholastic standards to determine eligibility for loans by the Federal government had been taken out of the Act and that they were being given to the provinces by the amendments. (a)	to have attained a satisfactory scholastic standard, and

The important thing to keep in mind in raising points for consideration by the government on this-and hon. members have made very useful points along the lines that were also raised in the earlier stages of the debate-is that the provincial ministers of education are carrying out a complete review of all student aid programs. The cost of it would be $4 million for the Canadian section and $2 million for the U.S. section. Why it is more expensive per mile in the United States than in Canada is difficult to understand. An hon. member who sits close by says that the reason for this is that the terrain there is rocky.
This leads me to the other argument made by the company when they were asked why the route did not go through Canada. The company pointed out that the alternate route would be from the Trans-Canada line through the edge of the Canadian shield and thus would be plagued by both water and rocks, which was not felt to be advantageous. This might not be the real reason for the route not crossing Canada, and this raises a problem which I wish to mention. The reason that the route is brought down through the United States is that this company intends to sell a considerable amount of gas in the United States. They have established a U.S. company to work in co-operation with the newly established Canadian company, both companies being held by Inter City Gas. The reason for this is that there is a lucrative market for gas in the United States and only a limited one in Canada. For this reason, I believe that the representative of the company would have been more accurate if he had stressed the fact that money would be derived from the route in the United States.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
As we all know, there is a very limited market in that area. It is probable that the only reason the pipeline is coming back into Canada is to serve the new pulp and paper complex in the Fort Frances area. We are not

opposed to this. In fact, we are pleased that this particular development is taking place and that gas can be brought in to make feasible the operation of that pulp and paper complex in the Fort Frances area.
I think one weakness of the committee discussion is the inability or lack of desire to find out the comparison in cost in terms of the service to Canada from this pipeline. I am not sure from reading the report what the distance would be as I do not know whether it is to be brought directly into the Fort Frances area from the Trans-Canada pipeline or brought from south of Winnipeg into the Fort Frances area. This is an important matter and obviously will have some relationship to the cost per cubic foot in terms of gas delivered to the Canadian pulp and paper complex at Fort Frances and the difference that will be created by the amount of gas sold in the United States from points along that pipe line. It is unlikely it will pass through a number of communities without some sales being made.
I have been pleased to note that in the main this is a Canadian operation, with a large percentage of the shares held by Canadians, approximately ten to one, and that it has been quite successful in selling gas in Minnesota and southern Manitoba. I have always been concerned with the choice of a route for either a gas or oil pipeline. We will again be faced with this problem when we consider developing an oil line across Canada to serve the eastern markets.
It seems that we are depending entirely on the National Energy Board to make the assessment of whether the costs justify the means or whether the company should decide where to build a pipeline on the basis of serving a larger area with larger sales. This shorter route should be weighed against the proposition of an all-Canadian route. There may be savings through lower cost, although there may be an increase in capital costs for installation purposes and the volume would be less than if it served a large number of communities.
I believe this company has a good record, Mr. Speaker. Obviously, it does since the committee has agreed to this proposal. However, I am still concerned about this matter. I did not have the opportunity that committee members had of seeing the map showing where the proposed structure would be. I do not know if it is to be built from the Trans-Canada pipeline on the north to the city of Fort Frances on the south, nor am I aware of
January 29, 1970

the additional route that would be necessary to bring it to Fort Frances from the south. I am not in a position to even guess what the mileage would be nor am I in a position to guess at the total sales. Both of these will have some effect on the situation.
A company could legitimately argue that if they brought their pipeline in from the south, if they had an export permit and were allowed to sell a large volume of gas en route to the Fort Frances complex, the price would be lower. However, we know from experience this is not true. This has never happened. Gas is not a lower priced commodity because every person on the street uses it. It is the same price whether there are only one or two customers on the street or if everyone uses it. It is doubtful whether a large number of subscribers would substantially reduce the cost of gas to the Fort Frances complex as well as areas situated along the pipeline.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, it could be argued that if the pipeline were built entirely in Canada, although the capital cost would be considerably higher than using an alternative route, the capital cost would eventually be written off. Through our tax structure these companies are given considerable assistance. Much of their capital cost is written off over a period of time. There would then be a short pipeline. The National Energy Board would calculate the cost on the distance involved. The transportation costs would be reduced and eventually the ultimate consumer would have the benefit of a reduction in cost.
I am not very concerned about this bill. I know the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) is very interested in it because it affects his area. We are pleased that this development is taking place. It is taking place at a very good time. For a number of years there has been a very slack market for the pulp and paper industry. Apparently this has now changed for the better and many companies intend to get into production very shortly. I hope the building of this pipeline will be of assistance to them.
I ask hon. members to give consideration to an all-Canadian pipeline. I ask them to consider the advantages we will receive in terms of reduction of costs which is very important to the ultimate consumer. Also we will have control over this facility if it is totally under one agency. Mr. Graham, who represented the company, pointed out that there will be two sister companies, one to handle relations with the federal agency in the United States and the other to handle relations with the National
Private Bills
Energy Board in Canada. These companies will operate under significantly different criteria and often under legislation that is not necessarily designed to produce the same results. These two companies will be under the control of a third company, the parent company. Hon. members will agree this creates a complication which would not have arisen if the complete pipeline were built in Canada. When one or two committee members made inquiries about this matter, Mr. Graham commented that they had tentatively studied an alternate route but dismissed this. He did not have any figures to offer nor did he offer an alternative.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I think that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, after he gets over being pleased to have this gas coming into the area, may be concerned about the cost. Many factors contribute to cost and one would be the shorter distance in Canada; a second would be that capital costs will eventually be written off. The pipeline will operate as a transportation facility long after the capital is repaid.
The fact that we ask questions about the ownership and control of the company by Canadians means little when we cannot write in and are not writing into the corporations act any limitations on the sale of shares. It is not like the banks and life insurance companies where we have legislation to ensure that the situation does not change. If the 300-odd Canadian shareholders should decide to sell out, then the situation would be changed.
While I am not particularly concerned with this company, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned with the attitude of some Canadians and of some members of Parliament to this over-all problem. It is my opinion that we will have to face a very serious decision in the next few years regarding a new transcontinental oil line. It is my hope that the things that make up the desires and aspirations of a nation will be taken into consideration, as well as the fact that a particular company may not want to go through the rock and water of northern Ontario but would rather detour through the United States. This would mean that a foreign agency would be able to control one of our natural resources. Hon. members should give some consideration to this, not particularly because of this bill but because this bill does, in a small way, point out many of the problems we are going to have with pipelines in the future.

January 29, 1970
Private Bills

Mr. Speaker, in dealing with Bill S-17 on third reading, it was noted in testimony that the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) would make a correction in Hansard which I expected he would do when he closed the debate.
In a debate we had in the Committee on Transport and Communications, various things came up upon which most of us agreed. However, the basic philosophy concerning the transportation of natural resources in our country through another country and then back again to Canada is one with which I cannot agree. The pipeline is 160 miles long and 40 miles of that goes through Minnesota, then comes back to International Falls.
It seems to me when application is made by a corporation or pipeline company for a detour such as this feasibility studies should be available for the committee to consider possible alternate routes. In this particular case, there was no feasibility study made as far as building the pipeline directly from the Trans-Canada to the Canadian destination. I am very pleased to see that this company was quite prepared to table and add as an appendix, a list of the shareholders involved in the company. It is noteworthy that of 311,537 shares issued as outstanding, 307,836 are held by 817 shareholders resident in Canada and 3,701 shares are held by 20 shareholders in the United States. Mr. Speaker, I am sure none of us could have any objection to this type of corporation doing business in Canada with that type of corporate setup.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, looking at the route of the pipeline and remembering that we had a railroad trying to take our coal resources from the Kootenays to the United States and back to Roberts Bank, the analogy is too much to accept. The Great Northern would like nothing better than to obtain permission to take this coal through the United States and back to Roberts Bank. In this case, the Canadian Pacific would be left out in the distance somewhere. It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that I have reservations about this bill before us.
We will be very glad that this pipeline will serve a portion of Manitoba which has not got natural gas at the moment, but surely feeder lines could have provided service if this pipeline company or any other were interested.
Another point that bothers me is the amount of money being spent on labour. At page 7.8 in the transcript of the hearings, we

see that some $4 million will be spent in Canada and $2 million in the United States in the construction of the pipeline. I realize there are problems regarding employment of Canadians across the border, but it is only in the last few years that the United States immigration department has become so strict about visas for people working there on contracts allotted to and tendered by Canadian companies. As a result, they could not keep their employees on the United States portions of a particular job. Co-operation between Canada and the United States should relieve this situation so that our labour could complete the whole 160 miles of this pipeline without having to subcontract the 40-mile section through the United States.
I realize that there is also a problem as far as the union is concerned, but this too should be rectified. There should not be any restrictions on Canadian workers in the United States on a project such as this, any more than if a United States firm had the same opportunities here. We all appreciate that there are hardly any pipeline construction companies in Canada which are subject to United States domination1 in so far as the Construction contract is concerned. I am sure that all those bidding on this particular line would like to see it a completely Canadian job. I was very pleased to learn, through the evidence brought forth before the committee, that the pipe at least will be constructed by some Canadian company. This will give employment in Canada which, of course, is one of our main concerns.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to be consistent in our desire to have pipelines in Canada, then the next pipeline built, which will be one to serve the east, should be constructed by an all-Canadian group. While this .one does serve a section of Minnesota and comes back into Canada some problems exist, namely that we are using the territory of another country, as well as its labour, for the transportation of our natural resource. However, I for one will never take exception to the route because I am pleased to say that this particular company has its domain in Winnipeg and its major shareholders are in Canada. This is something we can appreciate at this particular time.

I have often said that such studies ought to be tendered for, and if this government were really interested in participatory democracy it would make sure that tenders are submitted. Governments feel increasingly a compulsion to compel: the single issue of environmental pollution wiR shortly oblige every citizen to comply with government regulations affecting cherished private routines of living.
In these circumstances, governments must acquire the power to speak persuasively and continuously, on many subjects and at many levels of comprehension. Where there is little or no public opinion there is likely to be bad government, which sooner or later becomes autocratic government." The same thing applied to these tenders and studies. If the government requires steel of a certain size and weight, it is a simple matter to ask for tenders. But if it is seeking information which cannot be so easily specified, the situation becomes more complex. The government would be justified in calling for public tenders for supplies of paper or books. Having had some experience in the field of market research and research in general, I should like to point out to the hon. member that a research project is not outlined at the outset. The government or the institution concerned does not say; "Ask these questions; interview these people."
What happens is that firms of consultants are invited to make proposals. These proposals outline the type of research it is intended to conduct in order to find the answers to certain questions, together with an estimate of the cost. Some proposals may be double the cost of others. On the other hand, if what is wanted in an answer to a question, some firms might interview two persons and others would interview a thousand. The customer must decide whether, regardless of the cost, one firm or the other is likely to produce the right answer. Once this decision is made, the customer cannot go to another firm and say; "This proposal came from another firm, but you can do it cheaper." That is not the way in which it is done. If the hon. member would examine the way in which the research and consultative studies industry has developed, he will find that the tender system was dropped some years ago because it had been found to be an utter failure.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL MARKS AND STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that hon. members will understand the degree of satisfaction that I take in being able to introduce and explain to some extent the measure which is now before the House. It has been quite a while since we began our planning for what might be properly described as this auto safety bill, but I think it is one of the more important measures that hon. members will be called upon to enact during the present
January 29, 1970

session and I am sure also that it will receive widespread endorsement in all parts of the House.
On June 17 I indicated that the government was giving consideration to legislation to establish mandatory safety standards for new motor vehicles and their components at the point of manufacture or of importation into Canada. The main reason for this legislation is the government's awareness of and concern about the seriousness of the highway accident situation and about the danger to the health of citizens which may result from motor vehicle exhaust and possible noise emissions.
In this connection I may say that this is not merely a highway safety bill in the rather confined definition of that word, but in fact it will go beyond that particular objective in order to take the first steps at least in terms of emissions from automobiles that can be a danger to health. I hope in my introductory remarks to illustrate to hon. members in a few moments just how we propose to do this.
The federal government has evidence that significant reductions in motor vehicle traffic accidents, injuries and deaths can be effected through the provision of safety standards for motor vehicles and components at the point of manufacture. This is clearly the most logical point at which to attack the problem to ensure that when the automobile leaves the factory in the first instance it is as safe as it is possible for those involved, from a technological and now from a legislative point of view, to devise. Therefore, we have this legislation coupled, incidentally, with the research program which my department is undertaking, and I am confident that this should contribute significantly to increased safety in motor vehicle transportation in Canada.
The legislation itself deals primarily with those parts of the highway safety program which are designed to improve the calibre of the automobile, but I want to emphasize that simultaneously we are undertaking a stepped-up research program into all aspects of highway safety. Of course, in some respects this is perhaps even more important than the standards of the automobile itself because it is only after an automobile becomes involved in an accident that the safety measures can, in effect, come into play. What we really have to find answers to before we can move truly, in a major way, into the field of solution and improvement is what it is that causes accidents in the first instance.
While a good deal of publicity is often given to the drunken driver or the impaired
Motor Vemcle Safety
driver, and while we have taken steps in an effort to improve that situation through the breathalyzer test, it is still a fact that a great deal is unknown about what causes drivers to become involved in accidents under circumstances which do not appear, on the surface at least, to contribute in any way to the actual crash.
So in addition to moving on the legislative front, through these efforts, to improve the safety standards of the vehicle itself, we will be moving as well-I am sure hon. members will get details of this at the committee stage-to step up our research efforts, because in the last analysis the prevention of accidents is the most important consideration.
In preparing this bill we recognized the need for close consultation with the provincial departments responsible for road and motor vehicle administration. As you are aware, sir, the provinces have primary responsibility for roads and road traffic as well as motor vehicle and driver registration. Here, if I may be permitted, I should like to pay tribute to the provincial ministers concerned who have shown at least as much interest in this matter as the federal government. They have also co-operated with us in every way-as the debate will undoubtedly reveal, and the subsequent questioning in committee-in order to ensure the maximum amount of co-operation between the two levels of government, because the federal effort alone would not be sufficient to make a significant improvement.
The federal-provincial discussions to which I have referred led to my meeting with the provincial ministers on September 4, 1969, when it was agreed that the federal government should assume responsibility for the safety standards for new motor vehicles manufactured in Canada and for motor vehicles imported into Canada. At this time it was also agreed that the provinces, under existing legislation, would undertake to ensure the safety of vehicles in use as well as the safety of replacement and additional parts for motor vehicles.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I think there was unanimous agreement that at the federal level we could make the biggest impact on the problem by dealing with the new car manufacturer, to ensure that as cars left the factory they were in top condition. It was also agreed that we would work closely with the provinces to ensure, wherever necessary, that they would introduce the kind of legislation which would
January 29, 1970

Motor Vehicle Safety put their needs on all fours with ours in terms of replacement parts. The provincial ministers indicated their support of the objectives in this field and the means contemplated to impose them, and it was agreed that the federal government should proceed with its legislation as quickly as possible.
The measure that I have the honour to introduce tonight, Mr. Speaker, is a bill which the provinces and the appropriate provincial ministers have said is desirable and one with which they are wholly prepared to co-operate.
At this stage I think it is important that I set forth with some care the principle of the bill. The bill defines a "motor vehicle" as, "any vehicle designed to be driven or drawn on roads by any means other than muscular power." It does not include vehicles designed for running on rails. Perhaps the operative words are, " 'motor vehicle' means any vehicle designed to be driven or drawn on roads". In a sense, that is the outside limit of the definition.
I am sure subsequent discussion will bring out that this puts us in a somewhat uncertain position with regard to some new types of vehicles now being introduced. I refer specifically to perhaps the most remarkable phenomenon in the new automotive age, the snowmobile and the snowcruiser-that kind of vehicle. We have had discussions with the provinces as to how this kind of machine might be brought under control. At the moment, however, there is such a conflict in the various forms of jurisdiction across the country that it was not deemed advisable to do it now. Nevertheless, the legislation does provide the means by which at some future time these modes of travel to which I have referred, the off-highway vehicle and various others, can be brought within the ambit of this legislation.
The act distinguishes between a manufacturer, distributor and importer. Here I get into some legal jargon with regard to persons engaged in the business of manufacturing, distributing and importing, respectively. I think these three categories are quite important in terms of legislation. Manufacturing, of course, includes the process of assembly.
The bill would give the government of Canada the authority to prescribe safety standards which would regulate the design, construction and functioning of motor vehicles and their components for the purpose of protecting persons against personal injury, impairment of health or death. I want to emphasize again the impairment of health
[Mr. Jamieson.}

provision, which I think will prove to be extremely important. Twenty-nine standards have now been prepared which can be adopted as the initial regulations under this legislation. In other words, Mr. Speaker, if and when this honourable House chooses to pass this legislation, there are now 29 standards which officials of the Department of Transport have established and which could be introduced immediately as the first set of regulations under this measure. Subsequently, of course, there will be others as new devices are discovered, but 29 are now in place and can be introduced. I should be very pleased to make copies available to hon. members who may wish to comment upon them. The bill would give this authority to the government under these 29 standards.
These standards deal with the main safety features which would be henceforth incorporated in all new motor vehicles for sale in Canada. As of the time of implementation, they would automatically become the standard and the starting point for the new legislation. For obvious reasons-and this is one of the matters which has concerned me a good deal in planning for this legislation, and I think it will also concern other hon. members-the initial standards will be identical in intent to those currently enforced in the United States.
The reason for this, of course, is the tremendous interchange of automobiles back and forth across the border. Indeed, the situation at the moment is that many automobiles manufactured in Canada are not in fact sold to Canadians, and a great many of the automobiles bought by Canadians are manufactured in the United States. Because of this transborder traffic it is necessary at the present time to have our regulations more or less on all fours with those of the United States.
I would like to emphasize, however, that some standards could be altered to conform with special Canadian requirements, and others may be added as the need arises. The most obvious would be some necessary provision for winter conditions in this country, which might not be necessary on some cars sold in the United States. Indeed, at some point we might have to modify these regulations so that cars being sold out of Canadian plants to the tropics would not be required, as they would be under the regulations, to be sold with heating equipment. As a first step it was felt desirable to keep them on the same basis and eventually, hopefully, to introduce special conditions for Canada where they were considered necessary.

It is hoped that the initial regulation can be published in March or April, and thereby-become effective at the commencement of production of the 1971 model vehicles. In other words, there is a rather important timetable, and I am quite confident that members will recognize this. I am sure if the legislation commends itself to the House at all, it will be law by that time. It is therefore important that we have the necessary authority to indicate to the manufacturers what the regulations will be, in time for the 1971 car year which begins quite a bit ahead of the point at which vehicles are put on sale.

So we have tried to be as all-embracing as possible in introducing these two measures. The noise problem is a little more difficult to cope with, particularly in terms of snowmobiles and so forth, but as one hon. member and I agreed this afternoon, noise emission might be the biggest single factor.
The act will establish national safety margins as trademarks which are the exclusive property of Canada. Under the act regulations will be made respecting the use of the national safety mark on prescribed classes of vehicles, such as passenger cars, multipurpose passenger vehicles, trucks, buses and motorcycles. The use of the mark-I wish to emphasize this-will imply compliance of the motor vehicle and its components with the prescribed safety standards.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It is not, if I may use an old phrase, a good housekeeping seal of approval. It does not say, in effect, "This vehicle has been inspected and has been approved by inspectors appointed under the act." The onus and the responsibility is on the manufacturer to show, by the application of this mark, that he has in fact complied with the conditions set down in such regulations as may be operable at any given moment. The form of this mark, as well as its location on the vehicle, will also be prescribed, together with the date of manufacture. Misuse of the national safety mark will be an offence. In passing, may I note that the bill provides for stiff penalties ranging from $5,000 to as much as $200,000 if convicted of offences under the act.
Manufacturers and distributors are prohibited from applying the national safety mark to motor vehicles, or from selling or possessing motor vehicles, to which has been applied the national safety mark unless those vehicles and their components comply with all safety standards applicable at the time the vehicle was manufactured. In other words, they cannot have vehicles in their possession unless these conditions have been met.
Manufacturers and distributors are also prohibited from exporting or from sending or conveying from one province to another motor vehicles to which the national safety mark has not been applied. Therefore, in the interests of Canada's good name and prestige abroad, while we are saying that we will have minimum requirements for Canada, we are also saying that we will not sell a less
2998	COMMONS
Motor Vehicle Safety
satisfactory car in any part of the world. As I said a few moments ago, the only distinction is in the possibility that when cars are to be sold in tropical countries, we might not require heating equipment in them.
Safety standards will also be prescribed for motor vehicles imported into Canada. This, again, is a most important consideration. These standards will also very probably be identical to those applicable to cars manufactured in Canada. All imported vehicles and their components will be required at the time of importation to comply with the prescribed safety standards applicable at the time the vehicles were manufactured. Hence, vehicles manufactured after the proclamation of this act could be imported only if they complied with the regulations. Individuals or companies importing new or used vehicles will be required to produce evidence at the time of importation demonstrating compliance with the regulations applicable when the vehicle was manufactured.
These safety standard regulations will not apply, however, to vehicles being brought into Canada temporarily for the purposes of exhibition and demonstration, nor to vehicles being used by tourists or visitors entering or passing through Canada. In the latter case I suspect that most vehicles will come in from the United States and, since the regulations in Canada and in the United States will be more or less similar, I do not foresee any difficulty being created.
The act will make it an offence for manufacturers, distributors or importers to fail to give notice of any defect. This, too, is a most important provision. This requirement applies when the manufacturer, distributor or importer is aware of the vehicle defect affecting safety. They are then required to furnish a notice to persons who have purchased the vehicles from them, to subsequent purchasers to whom warrantees have been transferred, and also to the Minister of Transport.
Incidentally, in my arrangements with the provincial ministers I have undertaken that immediately I or whoever the minister of transport may be receives the notification, it will be passed on to the appropriate provincial minister to take whatever action is deemed necessary within the provincial jurisdiction. These notices are to be sent by registered mail and will contain a description of the defect and the evaluation of the safety risk, as well as a statement of the means to be taken to correct the defect. It will not be a notice simply telling someone that his car is

inadequate. The companies will have to tell those people just how much risk the defect involves, and what they must do in order to correct it.

This is with respect to safety standard.

This provision will thus prevent the incorporation of any possible technical errors in our regulations and will also allow industry some time to ensure that their products comply with the regulations. We think this is a reasonable provision in view of the fact that many of the regulations promulgated under the act will require the expenditure of hundreds of thousands, and perhaps millions of dollars. We think it right to give manufacturers and other interested parties, which includes the general public, an opportunity to make submissions before the regulations become law.

The act will provide the government with power to enter places where motor vehicles and their components are manufactured or stored, for the purpose of inspecting both vehicles and applicable records. The act will also provide for the seizure, detention and forfeiture of vehicles found to be in violation of its provisions. The act will, further, specify penalties for violations of various provisions by either corporations or individuals, under both summary conviction and conviction by indictment. As I mentioned a moment ago, the bill provides a scale of penalties ranging up to $200,000 for some violations.
I hope this is a reasonably comprehensive summary of what is involved in the bill. I consider it a major step forward in what is undeniably one of the many serious problems facing us in this country and, indeed, the peoples of all civilized countries of the world. This House spends a good deal of time, understandably, discussing the loss of life which results from tragedies such as war and conflict. But the simple truth is that the car-
January 29, 1970



nage on our highways, the loss of life as a result of accidents, is of major proportions. Motor vehicle accidents are one of the major killers of modern man. It has taken a long time-perhaps many hon. members will say too long-for us to get this legislation together. It has not been an easy task. But I believe we have come up with a satisfactory and productive approach to this major problem.
I do not wish to end without again emphasizing that from my studies of this matter over recent months it has become apparent to me that there is a great lack of information concerning the causes of accidents and a great need for research into this matter. No matter how good the automobile is in the first instance, it will not get into trouble unless there is some action or reaction on the part of the person behind the wheel. There is a surprising lack of knowledge about the motivations of people who get into accidents. Are there really people who are accident prone? Should we have a more comprehensive driver's test and a more frequent reassessment of drivers? Should we, instead of advocating simply that people who drink should not drive, also advocate that people who are emotionally disturbed should not drive?
There are all manner of items in this category which remain woefully unresearched at the present time, but I think it is vitally important that we introduce this legislation now and make the regulations as stringent as possible. However, it would be a ghastly mistake if we as legislators were to leave the matter there and say we have done our part. The responsibility, in the last analysis, rests upon us to see that the necessary research is undertaken in order that we may find out why accidents happen.
It is not merely, as we are beginning to find out, the drinking driver who fits into the category of the accident prone driver; there are thousands of other causes for accidents. Therefore, hand in hand with this legislation, which I commend to hon. members, is my undertaking to the House that within our department we will step up considerably our research efforts.

I am looking forward to outlining in more detail in committee the nature of some of these projects. I am grateful to hon. members for the kind comments they made about this bill when it was given first reading. I hope that with their help we can make it law and extend its benefits to the people of Canada as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all listened with much interest to the minister's interpretation of this bill. He did a capable job. I want to fill in some of the background by showing how the bill came to the House of Commons; how long ago it is since this issue was placed before Parliament.
The first and most important move made by this government in respect of highway safety was its action in making the breathalyzer test mandatory. I now have a further measure of satisfaction in the government presenting Bill C-137 to the House of Commons for approval, even with its inadequacies and after long delay. My satisfaction arises from the fact that I took the initiative in introducing highway safety to the House of Commons and appealed to the government to accept some of the responsibility for reducing the tragic toll being taken on our highways in terms of death and injury. To introduce the question to the House of Commons, on November 19, 1963, I put this question to the prime minister of the day:
Would the Prime Minister take the first opportunity to make a television appeal to the Canadian people in order to impress upon them the great necessity for better observance of highway safety regulations, in the hope that we might reduce the traffic death toll which was so much in evidence last week end?
He replied:
I would be glad to do anything I can along the lines suggested by the hon. member, including an appeal over television if that were appropriate in the circumstances.

To my knowledge, nothing was done. Therefore, on April 16, 1964, I made another approach by asking the Minister of National Health and Welfare the following question:
Is any research being carried on by the minister's department with a view to discovering ways and means of curbing air pollution by vehicular traffic which is becoming an increasingly serious threat to the health of our nation.
The minister replied:
My department is conducting research into air pollution generally and we are keeping a close eye on efforts aimed at reducing noxious gases from internal combustion engines. We are also in close contact with United States public health service which is spending vast amounts of money on this problem and we are expecting to benefit from any developments which may take place there. Also automobile manufacturers in Canada and the United States have intensive research projects under way with a view to introducing measures to control pollution.
As the records show, with each succeeding month the death toll on the highways has increased. Therefore, in the hope of arousing some action, on June 2, 1965, I put this question to the then prime minister:
Owing to the ever increasing death toll on the highways, will the Prime Minister consider introducing legislation making it compulsory for automobiles being sold in Canada to be equipped with safety devices currently proven practical and efficient?
He replied:
This is a very important question and I think it should be put on the order paper so it can be studied.
I put the question on the order paper and it was replied to by the minister of industry in the following manner:
It should be emphasized that the provincial governments have the responsibility of drafting and enforcing regulations pertaining to the operational standards of motor vehicles. A great deal of work has already been undertaken by various groups to determine the areas where improvement in design or vehicle construction could lead to greater safety which would be useful in the preparation of a safety code. It would, of course, be necessary to obtain the agreement of the provinces before a uniform safety code could be established for motor vehicles. The Department of Industry would be happy to co-operate with the provinces in the preparation of such a code.
On January 27, 1966, I directed this question to the minister of justice:
Would the government give consideration to amending the Criminal Code so that the breathalyzer test can be made mandatory?
The minister stated:
That is one of the several possible amendments to the Criminal Code which are now being given consideration by the government.

This measure will be placed on the statute books. On February 2, 1966, on a supply motion, I spoke on highway safety. I will read into the record the following excerpt:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of highway safety deserves immediate attention. The federal government has failed to take the necessary steps to fulfil its obligations in fighting public enemy No. 1, the constantly increasing death toll on our highways. We are all aware of the appalling increase in highway accidents but it would seem these are being treated in some quarters as a course of events that should be expected. Something must be done and there should be no delay.
In my opinion, help and assistance would be readily available if this government would take the initiative and launch an all-out crusade to face up to this monster once and for all. They should pull out all stops, make the breathalizer test mandatory and increase the grant to the Canadian Highway Safety Council. A conference should also be called with provincial representatives and, in fact, representatives from all organizations willing to get together in a drive to bring about improvement in the situation.
Responsibility in highway safety has been ignored too long by all governments. Our laws and regulations have not kept pace with the times. Uniformity of laws and regulations, as well as of penalties, should apply to all provinces. Traffic signs and driver testing or any other feature having to do with our highways or driving on them should be the same.
Periodical vehicle inspection should be compulsory. Signboards, radio and television should be in constant use in an effort to keep our people alert and aware of the need for extreme caution on our streets and highways. No doubt if the people I have suggested were brought together to set up a framework or a pattern for greater highway safety, many worthwhile ideas would be brought to light.
Automobile manufacturers have shown a favourable response to highway safety through their willingness to supply cars for student training and supply them in abundance. Their designers are constantly investigating safety features and quite a number have been included in car equipment with satisfactory results. Perhaps the automobile people could be persuaded to go quite a lot further by way of extensive research on some of the recently suggested safety devices.
I suggest that in the not too distant future legislation will necessarly be passed to make antismog equipment a requirement. There is no way of assessing the injury being inflicted on us by carbon monoxide. However, we do know that any element which causes irritation in the lungs is a potential contributor to lung cancer. We know too that carbon monoxide is deadly when confined and may even be the cause of some highway accidents.

On February 16, March 23, and April 1, 1966, I put questions to ministers on the matter. In these questions I continued to press for some action. On May 2, 1966, I put this question on the order papers:
Has the government received representations from any provincial government or association or other

organized body asking for the calling of a federal-provincial conference for the purpose of working out a national program:

Has the government taken any action in regard to the promotion of highway safety and, if so, what action?
The minister replied:
Yes. In so far as the departments of defence production and industry are concerned: (1) The Canadian government specifications board has prepared a draft automotive vehicle safety code in collaboration with the Canadian Good Roads Association and the traffic injury research foundation. The draft has been submitted for critical review to a committee consisting of representatives of the provinces, the motor vehicle manufacturers, safety groups, the medical profession and others. A revised draft is now being prepared.
(2)	The government has undertaken to include all available safety features in the specifications governing the procurement of conventional type vehicles for both civilian departments and the military.
(3)	Two consultants have been engaged: one to assist on the automotive safety code and the other to conduct research studies.
(4)	Consideration is being given to what other steps the federal government can usefully take in the light of the constitutional position and the relative responsibilities of the provinces and the government in this area.
Further... in so far as requiring of pollution control devices for motor vehicle exhaust systems is concerned, the committee recommended that the standard for the pollutants omission control be deleted from the proposed standards because: (a) it is not yet agreed that this is indeed a safety device, (b) the Department of National Health and Welfare is making a detailed study of the problem of air contamination in close consultation with their counterparts in the United States.
I could continue to enumerate many more questions asked by myself and others in the House of Commons who joined in the dialogue about that time, but I think I have

made it clear to the House that the government showed much reluctance and indifference to a problem that was costing the country thousands of lives and millions of dollars.
However, the justice committee did table a report on March 27, 1967. The report was dated March 21 and a release concerning its contents read as follows:
Government intervention in the area of auto safety was today recommended by the Commons Justice Committee, when it tabled its report to the House.
The chairman ... said the main recommendation of the committee was to establish a public board. This board, with representatives from the federal government, the automotive industry, the provincial governments and universities, would be charged with the responsibility for "developing, as quickly as possible, and improving from time to time the appropriate safety standards of design of construction and equipment for all motor vehicles produced in or imported into Canada, and authorized for use in interprovincial or international transportation". Safety standards would be more in the nature of performance standards, rather than specific items of equipment.
In addition the board would be charged with the "authority to set appropriate standards on inspection and quality control' and see that they are observed by automotive producers and parts manufacturers. It would initiate the supervising of traffic safety research possibly through the National Research Council. Co-ordination of the activities of the many voluntary governmental agencies now interested in and involved in traffic safety would also be one of its functions.
The report went on to say that while this board should be established by federal legislation it is essential that the co-operation of the provincial governments and the automotive industry be obtained and that "the danger of bureaucratic control over this vital industry should be minimized". The committee's report is based on ten months of hearings, study and investigation.
At the end of November 1966 the committee made a three day visit to the Detroit-Windsor area during which they visited the laboratory and automobile testing facilities of General Motors at Milford, Mich., Ford Motor Company in Dearborn, Mich., and Chrysler Motor Company at Highland Park, Mich. The committee had two meetings while in Windsor at the University of Windsor, at which the executives from the major automobile manufacturers were questioned.
Among the many witnesses who appeared before the committee were the Canadian Automobile Association; Canadian Government Specifications Board; Canadian Labour Congress the United Automobile Workers Union.
Among the 33 documents filed with the committee was information required by the committee of the automotive manufacturers showing recall campaign figures for the last five years.
The Chairman said he felt that the Committee's recommendations would go far in answering the problem of auto safety with all its many facets. Just as important as safety devices in automotive vehicles is the co-ordination of the many voluntary agencies which are involved in education and research in traffic. From the evidence given before the committee, it would appear that there was a

definite deficiency in this area. He also pointed out that the committee does not recommend specific safety devices, but rather recommends that the public agency enforce performance standards; and quality control and production procedures. The committee was considering two private bills bringing safety devices under the Criminal Code, and four notices of motion recommending that the government take action in this area.
At his point I would like to read into the record three clippings ol recent date that I think are timely. The first, taken from the Ottawa Journal, is dated November 28, 1969:
An executive of one of the largest automobile insurance companies in the United States predicts that within a few years insurers will set their rates according to how susceptible to damage the automobile is.
Sweden already has such a system, and reports it working well. As a preliminary move to consideration of the innovation in the U.S., the National Assocation of Independent Insurers hired a professor from the University of Detroit to determine how susceptible various cars are to damage.
Those involved in the study estimate it may be a year or more until enough data have been accumulated to make any evaluation. But they apparently agree on one point-that modern cars, particularly their bumpers, are not being made as collision-proof as they could be, or once were.
Automobile insurance premiums directly reflect the rising cost of automobile repairs. It is natural that insurers should try to place a higher cost of insurability on those products which accidents statistics and tests indicate provide the least resistance to damage.
This move might produce consternation among automobile manufacturers, but it could also be the strongest possible incentive to produce cars which not only look pretty but wear well.
The next clipping is taken from the Toronto Telegram of January 14, 1970. It is a press release from Detroit, and reads as follows:
A group of automotive engineers squirmed uncomfortably in their seats as an insurance safety executive stopped just short of calling them criminals.
Doctor William Haddon Jr., president of the Washington-based Insurance Institute for Highway Safety was talking about high performance, high powered cars.
"The way the auto industry is pushing muscle cars borders on criminal irresponsibility," said Dr. Haddon.
He acted as moderator for a panel discussion at the Society of Automotive Engineers Congress, which dealt with how to reduce highway losses.
"Cars with high horsepower ratings are fine on the racetrack, but it's almost criminal to use them on public roads."
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Dr. Haddon was referring to such juiced-up packages as the Pontiac GTO; the Plymouth Road Runner; and the Ford Torino Cobra.
Muscle cars, or supercars, or factory hotrods as they are often called, accounted for 600,000 sales last year.

"Due to advertising techniques, the image that is being sold at great expense to the buying public is why you don't have transportation, you have thrills on the highways."
Dr. Haddon said insurance losses are substantially higher on muscle cars.
"We don't know if this is because of the way they are built, or because they are used too fast" said the safety expert.
Supercars are responsible for a credibility gap involving safety and the auto industry.
"I know these cars are not the way for American business to protect the capitalistic system in the generation now coming of age in the decade of the 70s," said Dr. Haddon.
He was asked after the panel session what the future holds.
"It's the automaker's choice. They are either going to face condemnation by the public and probably restrictions by the government."

He was also critical of reports that car makers are turning away from development of safety seats with built-in belts.
