I have a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of January 28, 1970. This release is from Worcester, Massachusetts. It states:
An experimental car that would be safe in any kind of crash up to 50 mph will be built and tested within the next three years, Transportation Secretary Volpe said Tuesday.
Volpe said the "mobile crash laboratory" being planned could be rolled over at 70 mph with its passenger compartment remaining intact.
The car would offer improved handling, braking and visibility and use low-pollution fuels, he said.
"Our plan is to have 14 of these cars and tested by the end of 1972," he said. "It is our intention that the auto industry will seize on the new safety improvements we develop and incorporate them in production models."
I should now like to return to the bill. Regulations covering national safety standards for automobiles are long overdue, but I am afraid, however encouraging this bill appears at first sight, it falls considerably short of its objectives. I cannot quarrel with the fact that specifications or standards are not spelled out in this bill, although I shall have some comments later on that. I question the strange omissions that could, in the hands of certain unscrupulous car dealers, lead to death or injury for the buyers of cars which bear the national safety mark but which in fact have been transformed into deathtraps.
There must be protection for the innocent person who is lured into buying a car carrying the national seal of approval but which has become defective through wear, damage or tampering. There is nothing in the bill
January 29, 1970

which prohibits, after the initial sale, tampering or changing those parts of the auto which have met the approved safety standards. Failing this, an attempt should be made to encourage a voluntary system of standard controls within the used car trade.
We all appreciate that improved safety standards will add to the price of the automobile, but at least we will live longer. I am told that about half the cars now being produced will, during their life span, be involved in an injury-causing accident. Federal regulations can be made considerably stronger by an amendment which should be moved in committee, to the effect that this act shall apply to the shipment of motor vehicles, new or used, from one province to another, as though the shipment into the province were an import. A second amendment could be moved to the effect that the national safety mark be accompanied by the words, "As at the time of manufacture, assembly, importation and new car sale". The bill refers to components. I do not know whether this applies to tires or ashtrays. I believe the bill should spell out the difference between components and accessories, and that this must not be left to pure chance or individual interpretation of the safety code.
We have heard statements to the effect that Canadian standards to accompany this bill are similar to U.S. safety requirements, but I wonder just how compatible U.S. standards are for cars running on Canadian highways. South Carolina is different from Ontario. Consideration should be given to the climatic conditions, and in spelling out our safety standards we would be well advised to study the situation in countries which have conditions similar to those found in Canada. The bill is concerned primarily with the safety of the driver, the passenger, the pedestrian and the other driver. I hoped it would cover, by enforcement of strong, air pollution regulations, the safety of all persons in Canada.
History has shown time and again that major epidemics are stamped out only after major research efforts. At long last the public are beginning to realize that we are faced with an epidemic, the contributing factors being the driver, the road and the car. I am especially concerned with the third factor, the car. I do not suggest that the others are not just as important, but we in Parliament can control the car. This bill is not the answer to the problem.
With the exception of making the breathalyzer test mandatory, Bill C-137 is all we
Motor Vehicle Safety
have to show in response to the deep desire of the Canadian people for something that will be effective in achieving a maximum reduction of the death and destruction on our highways. This bill is indeed a very vague document and leaves much to be desired. It is to be hoped that when it goes to the committee, the necessary amendments will be made so that when it returns to the House it will be more specific and meaningful.

Mr. Speaker, the matter before us in Bill C-137 is safety standards for motor vehicles. This is potentially of extreme importance to millions of Canadians. Before dealing with some of the details of the proposals I should like to take a few moments to sketch-in the background of this matter.
The annual traffic toll now is 60,000 people killed and 3,650,000 injured-and many of the latter might as well be dead. In economic terms, this traffic toll represents a loss of approximately $2 million every hour of every day, of every week, of every month of every year. For our part, in Canada we kill 5,000 people every year and no less than 150,000 Canadians are injured, non-fatally, on our roads and highways. To put the last two figures in closer focus, let me put it this way: in a four-year period-say the life of a Parliament-20,000 Canadians die and 600,000 are injured on our roads.
There are three major factors involved in this warlike toll; the first is the car, the second is the driver and the third is the road condition. The bill we are considering tonight-and I compliment the minister for his very able introduction of it-seeks to do something to lower the death and injuries toll for which the car itself is specifically responsible. At this point it might be well for us to keep in mind that in North America there are now 100 million vehicles and that this number is increasing at the rate of about nine per minute.
Considering the toll and the economic drain involved in this highway war, it may be surprising that North Americans, Canadians included, have done so little to defend themselves against it. The fact is that on this continent we have all been assured for many years by the industry, which in many respects is as powerful as the nation, that what the industry wants is good for the public.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Inasmuch as the industry is producing cars for maximum sales, maximum profits and

January 29, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
quick obsolescence, this goodness to the public is not evident. The car consumer, dazzled by even greater sex, speed and prestige appeals, and having very little control over what is produced or offered to him in the way of a motor vehicle, has taken a long time to realize that public safety is more important than private profit. However, he has finally realized this; he is on the road. He has a long way to go, but in the United States and in our country legislation of this type is an indication that there has been a realization of the situation and of what will be attempted in the future.
Bill C-137 is designed to set safety standards on cars, trucks and motor cycles entering Canada or manufactured in Canada. I thought the minister and the previous speaker both did well in outlining some of the details of the legislation. The bill is a move in the right direction, but it has its weaknesses and shortcomings. We know that auto safety legislation will bear the United States stamp of approval, but the possibility of Canadian standards varying substantially from those in the United States I believe is small.
Canadian auto safety standards will be set in Washington, where the consistent opposition of the industry has slowed down progress in this field and where the United States authorities too often have tended to accept the standards the industry dictates. On that point, in fairness to the United States authorities, I should like to mention that I have in my hand a number of releases from the office of the secretary, Department of Transportation in the United States. These show an increased awareness of the need for speedy action in protecting the United States motoring public. These releases come to my desk almost daily, and I imagine they are received by other members. Here is one:
The federal highway administration plans to improve its motor vehicle safety standard 209 dealing with seat-belt assemblies.
This is another:
Secretary of Transportation John A. Volpe today announced release of the first of what will be a series of monthly reports to the public on the department's most recent vehicle safety compliance activities.
Then we have this release:
Secretary of Transportation John A. Volpe today demonstrated a modified diesel engine and exhaust system for transit buses which offers substantial improvements in eliminating pollutants, smoke, noise and odour.
I have several others. I thought I would take this opportunity to refer to the fact that

in the United States, and I hope here, the department of transport has finally become aware of the pressing need for such action and is working on it. It might be of interest to us as members of this House to think back to the genesis of the bill.
It had its genesis in a previous Parliament when with the consent of the government a number of hon. members, including the hon. member who spoke last, who had private member's bills on the Order Paper with relation to one phase or another of traffic safety, took their bills off the Order Paper. The subject matter of these bills was then referred to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. This committee held a great number of meetings at which many witnesses were heard.
This resulted in a report supported, I believe, by all members of the committee. The report finds some expression in the legislation before the House tonight. Incidentally, the proposal in respect of the breathalyzer test was part of the committee's report. I have gone into this background because as one of the members who took a bill off the Order Paper I believe that in respect of non-partisan matters this is a good way to have action taken in respect of proposals, and to have a solidified result come back to the House. That is what has happened today in respect of this bill. It also is what happened last year in respect of the breathalyzer legislation. There are areas of common thinking and common opinion in respect of which unified action can be taken which results in worth while legislation. My opinion is that this is a worth while process.
We have some criticism in respect of the bill. It would seem that safety features peculiar to the Canadian climate, such as rear window defrosters, are not likely to be included. The initial safety standards to which the bill refers are not spelled out. They are to be regulated by the Governor in Council. The 29 standards the minister mentioned are those which are now required by law in the United States. At present they act as a voluntary guide for the Canadian, United States-controlled auto industry. For the present we accept the 29 standards as a basis, but we must press for a much further extension of standards.
We want Canadian auto safety standards included specifically in this legislation. We should not despair of having this done. What can be done to force a general acceptance of standards is well illustrated by the action of New York state, where safety belts were
January 29. 1970

made mandatory. Safety belts soon became standard across the continent. The same thing happened when California established tough standards for hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide emissions from vehicle motors. The standards are important and are becoming more common.
I believe a similar situation could develop here if Canadian authorities had the courage to set proper standards and enforce them. Enough cars are sold in Canada to have a significant effect on the total market. Cars sold in Canada can be fitted with safety features even if Washington fails to act. I think it is a crying shame that one need today is for such standards in respect of bumpers. Originally these appendages were designed to protect cars and passengers in case of accident.
Today, with the industry's accent on eye appeal rather than safety, and with the drive for more and more profits, bumpers perform a dual function: they are decorative devices designed to sell cars through eye appeal, and they seem to be engineered to achieve the maximum sale of spare parts.
The fact is that the fancy chrome on the front and rear of most cars is not intended to perform the bumper function. There are no standards in respect of height, and the great variety of design and shine features are completely useless as protective devices. Worse than this, however, is the fact that many bumpers have knife-edge protrusions running vertically, horizontally or both, and some have protruding snouts with the knife edges coming to a point in front of the grille. Others have a bewildering variety of knobs, gadgets and fixtures which perform no useful function to the car or its owner. All these devices perform maximum damage to both cars involved in a collision.
As far back as December, 1966, the Canadian Government Specifications Board emphasized the need to design bumpers to meet their original protective function. The board called for a standard height, flat surfaces, and shock-resistant construction. The design of the New York state safety car included such a bumper. So far, the industry has ignored bumper safety and has continued to design eye catching, cosmetic and damage-prone chrome.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Canada can set realistic standards for bumpers sold in this country-standards relating to height, surface and shock resist-21611-51
Motor Vehicle Safety
ance. These standards should be set now, before designers of the 1972 models tell us that their new, devastating bumpers are locked into models beyond recall.
There are many phases and spheres involved in our discussion of this legislation- which is perhaps 15 or 20 years late-which is intended to grapple with car safety. There is the matter of air pollution and sound pollution in relation to the car, and I was glad to hear the minister refer to it. I remember raising the question last November in the House. I was assured by the minister's parliamentary secretary that under clauses of the proposed legislation there would be scope for prosecution in line with the legislating of vehicles whose function impairs the public health or welfare because of noise and air pollution. This is a point which we in this part of the House are most concerned about and will try to get spelled out in the legislation.
In working in the committee in trying to improve this legislation, we will keep in mind what has happened in the United States. We will think and act on the basis of the U.S. experience. We will remember that the car makers in the United States are charging higher prices, more than the actual cost of quality safety improvements. We will not forget that United States government-financed safety tests show that individual car component failures are at a rate of about 10 per cent, and we cannot overlook the fact that dozens of types of car tires have failed to comply with federal safety standards.
It seems to us important to remember that according to one expert at least, the average new car in North America has 25 to 40 defi-ciences, and that seat belts produced by 10 or 12 of the biggest U.S. suppliers are under investigation for what appears to be failure to meet federal standards. Let us consider this point for a minute. At 10 miles per hour, a crash between two standard model popular cars in the United States, such as you see driven around here every day, results in average estimated damage of $510 for both cars.
In addition, we believe that when we have set our car safety standards, they must not only be enforced but they must be seen to be enforced. We think that safety must not only be achieved but must be seen to be achieved by the public.
I would like to remind the minister of his reply to a question I asked last December 8. I asked, having in mind the U.S. regulation requiring manufacturers of automobiles to

January 29, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
provide the people of the U.S. with specific information and data on the safety qualities of their vehicles, whether the minister was giving consideration to similar legislation in this country. The minister replied:
I think this is a commendable step. As soon as we have the necessary authority and a bill is passed by this House I will be more than pleased to give it consideration ... X see no reason why we should not do so.
I think it is important, if we are to have this legislation, to convince the public that we mean business and that we are going to make it work. That is why I stress the need for open action by the administration.
In summary, and in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we support the general aim of the bill, noting its lateness and its weaknesses. It is our hope that in committee or in the House we will be able to strengthen the provisions of the bill so that they will work more for the benefit of the Canadian public. May I note, Mr. Speaker, that while I have been speaking, approximately 1,200 car accidents have taken place in North America, half a million dollars damage has been done, and 55 more cars have been produced.

Mr. Speaker, I did not expect I would have to speak today on Bill C-137. However, I want to make a few remarks on the principle of the bill and to assure the minister and the House that we, members of the Ralliement creditiste, are in favour of the principle of the bill and feel it will, to a certain extent, improve safety standards on our roads. I say "to a certain extent" because, as the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) said today, provincial governments, as the road network comes under their jurisdiction, are partly responsible for accidents occurring on them. We know to what extent roads in bad repair are responsible for accidents. Part of the responsibility for accidents must also be borne by drivers unaware of highway regulations or driving while their faculties are impaired by alcohol.
This bill also purports to improve vehicle safety standards to ensure the safety of drivers.
In order to illustrate the need for this bill, I would like to give the House information from the July-August 1969 issue of the Bulletin of the Canadian Highway Safety Council, where I found figures which do not tally with those supplied by the hon. member a moment

ago. In 1968, there were 4,370 fatal accidents in which 5,254 people died and 172,795 were injured.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Since so many people were injured or killed in the course of a single year, one can venture to say that more people are injured or kill on the highways than in any war.
In 1968 Canada reported 479,721 accidents in which people were injured or killed. That is enough to make us think and to prompt the government to take all the necessary measures to improve highway safety in Canada. That is its responsibility.
In 1959, for instance, 3,231 persons lost their lives and 84,445 were injured. In 1968, almost ten years later, 5,254 were killed and 172,795 were injured.
In view of the increasing number of accidents, the government was justified, even though it may have acted a little bit late, in taking appropriate measures to improve the safety of motor vehicles.
The minister said he had a list of 29 safety standards. Here is how the expression is defined in the bill:
-standards regulating the design, construction or functioning of motor vehicles and their components for the purpose of protecting persons against personal injury, impairment of health or death.
We must admit that since the appearance of the first automobile, there have been improvements in the construction of motor vehicles and the manufacturers, to a certain extent, are not too concerned about the safety of their products. Indeed, automobile manufacturers have often become big trusts more concerned with making profits than safer cars. Evidently, competition exists among car manufacturers and it prompts them to improve constantly the cars offered to their clients. However, it must also be realized that quite often we unfortunately have to pay for costly useless gadgets only to increase their profits.
I hope that the 29 security standards introduced by the minister have been selected so as to help the drivers rather than enable car manufacturers to make even more money.
I was saying a few minutes ago that the manufacturers have to a certain extent improved their vehicles from a safety point of view. For instance, the advent of shatterproof windshields was a great progress which surely prevented countless accidents. In spite of it, loss of life was caused by drivers travelling at excessive speed. However, there was continuous improvement of the braking
January 29, 1970

system on cars and today we have disck brakes. We have better suspension and steering systems in cars.
Power-steering and power-brakes have greatly improved motor vehicles as such.
Sometimes, though, new accessories appear on the market, such as tubeless tires, which, in my view, have come too soon, causing many accidents, fatal ones sometimes, when they blew out, as the product had not been perfected. Today, this danger no longer exists, because tires have been improved; but, for two or three years, the car driver had to try them out himself and he was the one who had to pay.
Despite all these improvements in the manufacture of cars, some control should be exercised at the drawing-board stage. Any prototype, after it is launched, should be sujected to an inspection. In fact, I believe that this bill provides for the appointment of inspectors; they should have the necessary authority to check the specifications of the new car before it is put on the market.
The rear lights of a certain make are placed in such a way that once snow-covered, they are almost invisible, which endangers the life of the driver and of the passengers in the cars behind.
These are points which a government-appointed inspector should verify before a car is built, so that the public might be protected against such hazards.
Mr. Speaker, these are the few remarks I wanted to make to show the importance of this bill. When it is deferred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, we will be able to get more information from the minister and the experts who will perhaps be invited to advise the committee members. If the bill does not meet with the wishes of the public, we will be able to ask the minister to bring in the necessary amendments.
I have just mentioned the efforts of the manufacturers in order to increase the safety of vehicles, but one should not forget the laws that the government has enacted for this purpose.
1 should like to deal at this stage with the breathalizer test which I think has not yet been applied long enough to permit us to appreciate its results, but I am convinced that it will bring an improvement on the roads. A similar provision has already been applied in England. While I was discussing it with an English Tory a few months ago he told me 21611-51$
Motor Vehicle Safety
that though he had been opposed to such a test he had to admit that it had greatly increased highway safety in England and that, therefore, the same results could be expected in our country.
The steps provided for in the bill are meant to increase highway safety. With the co-operation of automobile drivers, automobile insurance rates will decrease or, at least, will not increase, as they have over the past years.
For these reasons, we ought to concur in the motion for second reading and reference of the bill to a committee for study.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this piece of legislation. In all fairness, I think one should first point out that it is new legislation; it is not legislation which just re-enacts a measure which has been in operation. I was interested in the minister's remark that the department has gone to the trouble of researching 29 standards which will apply immediately the act is promulgated.
I was disappointed that clause 7 of the bill suggests that regulations will be drawn up. I think the 29 standards should have been examined more carefully, because I do not like buying a pig in a poke. I suppose we shall have to trust the judgment of those who will be responsible for administrating the 29 standards.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The minister dealt with the question of standards and said they will be much the same as those in the United States. Because of our different climatic conditions, our cold winters, our frosts, our methods of road-heating and so on, these standards may have to be adjusted.
The minister did not say what research would be conducted into these standards. Nowhere in the bill does it say that the branch of government responsible for research will examine the application of the 29 standards and ascertain whether, for instance, six or seven additional standards should be added in view of the winters and summers we have in this country. Before passing this legislation we should know whether bodies like the National Research Council will study these standards.
In the past the government has frowned on research, and there is an indication that this is the thinking with respect to this legislation. The former minister of transport set up what

January 29, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
was called, I believe, an engineering institute. It was given $250,000 and told to study road safety matters. That institute has not yet brought down its report; it is still being typed. But we have before us a piece of legislation dealing with this very matter.
Before the bill receives second reading and goes to committee, I ask this simple question: Will the members of this engineering institute, which cost $250,000 to set up, be heard by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, so that the committee may determine whether pertinent standards relating to highway hazards have been covered by this legislation? I bring my question to the attention of the minister, the chairman of the committee and to all hon. members of the House. We may derive some benefit from the studies of the institute.
According to the minister, these 29 standards are initial standards only and may be adjusted as time goes on. I throw the idea out that perhaps there should be a continuing study of this whole question. I think the engineering institute which was set up to study road safety matters should continue its study. All its members need not be kept on; perhaps only one or two of the university professors who worked on the original study should be retained. In any event, there should be a continuing examination of standards by a body whose job is to see whether this legislation will do what we want done.
As I said, it is a new piece of legislation; it is not a re-drafting or a re-enactment of something already on our statute books. Surely there is merit in having a body continuing a study of these standards. Similar bodies should undertake continuing studies of health standards, pollution standards and, as the minister suggested, noise standards.
The minister dealt partially with the question of farm tractors. He said that if they are licensed to go on highways, they will be covered, and if they are not so licensed, they may not be covered. As I understand it, any vehicle licensed to go on a highway will be covered by this legislation. The minister raised the question of snowmobiles which may or may not be licensed to go on highways. In many cases they are prohibited from going on highways. Many provinces across Canada are becoming increasingly concerned about the safety of snowmobiles and the hazards they pose to motorists and pedestrians. So far as I know, the bill does not deal with this matter; but perhaps members of the committee will examine it at the appropriate

time. I understand that the list of 29 standards referred to will be included in today's Hansard.
Another aspect of the bill which disturbs me may be considered in committee and will no doubt be considered by those who will be responsible for enforcing the act. Unquestionably, we must have guidelines or safety standards for the manufacturer or importer, but the question is: Should we apply those standards and penalties to a distributor? The manufacturer makes the product and ships it to someone to sell. The importer imports the product and hands it over to a distributor. I wonder whether we should police the distributor as well as the manufacturer and importer. I think that the less policing there is, the better.

We would then be calling the importer a distributor; that would be the effect. In my opinion an importer should import.
Let us consider farm tractors. Today component parts of farm tractors are being imported into Canada and the North American market in general and made into complete units. From my reading of the bill, it deals with component parts but not with the whole automobile. If a component part is unsafe, the inspector can make a decision about it.
Although these parts are sold by a distributor, one cannot say that in that sense he is the manufacturer; nor should he be treated as the manufacturer. I suggest that that aspect must be looked into, because I am concerned that some provision of this bill will apply to plain, ordinary distributors. [DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I am surprised that in connection with a major piece of legislation, one which will be on the statute books for a long time, the minister has not felt called upon to make provision for much greater continuity with regard to the process of inspection. I am surprised that no provision has been made for

the training of inspectors and the continuity of their employment. I have never been particularly in favour of expanding the civil service, but I would point out that knowledge and continuity are built into that organization, a regular body to which people are hired by a commission.

I recognize that the minister is a very competent and capable person, but I do not think his job allows him time in which to watch over the situation properly. This is a very important bill, Mr. Speaker, and I believe it will arouse a great deal of interest among Canadians. It is likely to have its ups and downs before it becomes effective in eliminating some of the carnage which takes place on our highways.
It is interesting to reflect that Mr. Ralph Nader and the United States "Consumer Report" have probably been more responsible for promoting recognition among the general public of the features which are unsafe in automobiles than have any of the investigations conducted in Canada or in the United States. The one thing which both depended

January 29, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
upon was the force of public opinion. In the course of this debate, during which a number of interesting comments were made, the National Press Club was not represented. There is a difference of opinion as to whether the attractive section of the press gallery can be counted part of that institution.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The public will not regard the safety measures being proposed as necessary unless they can be convinced that safety is a major factor in the preservation of their lives. While for the last five or six years I have not done very much travelling, I have been on the highway frequently and driven cars that were considered to have the safest possible equipment- for example, seat-belts. For four or five years I owned a Volvo and now I own another car. Although both of them had a safety-harness over the shoulder, I can honestly say that I never wore the harness in either car.
This is an admission that I am not convinced that this is necessary equipment or that it is a selling point. A number of people have asked me whether I consider the Volvo the safest vehicle on the road, and I have said it may be. They ask how I like the shoulder-harness, but I have had to reply that I have never tried _ it on. My son used it, but it seemed a difficult procedure.
My present car has a very elaborate safety-harness. It is an imported car and meets the safety standards not only of the United States but of European countries. I tried on the harness once but found it six or eight inches too short for me. But my point is that the public are not yet convinced that car safety is their business. Until the average man wants safety features in his automobile, I suggest our cars will not be safe.
We have always been suckers for United States advertising on television. We buy aspirins because people in the United States do. We buy Oldsmobiles because they do, and we even buy Cadillacs because they do. Continually we are bombarded with advertising claiming that U.S. cars are good cars and are the kind of cars that we should buy.
As a colleague of mine said the other day, although it is important to have safety devices on cars, it is equally important that we should be able to start our cars. Certainly we will not get into any trouble on the road if our cars do not start. My colleague was pointing out that the car that he had-and also the car I had at the time-was failing to start.
IMr. Peters.]
It seems to me that what is required is a car made in Canada which incorporates Canadian safety equipment. I recall driving down the Queensway the other night and observing in a distance of about eight blocks five or six cars that had stalled. This had created a traffic hazard that was serious, and it would have been quite easy to cause a 50-car pile-up. It seems to me that this is certainly a factor that should be taken into account when considering car safety.
For example, in Florida a car would probably require only 100 amps to start it. The battery will be required to deliver about 40 amps for roughly two and a half minutes, and then can settle down to supplying amperage to the coil, the points, the sparking plugs and all the rest of it. Gasoline that we buy in Canada does not burn well at a temperature of 40 below zero; it is primarily intended for climates warmer than ours. But I suggest that at least our cars should have installed in them batteries which are adequate for our conditions instead of those obtaining in the tropics.
I recall observing a car parked outside the building the other night which a member of the protective staff was helping to start. When he lifted the hood he found the wind had blown up under the car and covered the engine, the distributor and ignition wiring, with three or four inches of snow. Consequently, it would not start. After the snow was brushed away, the car started.
I remember the day when I used to drive model T Fords. I am a contemporary of other members here who did the same. As a kid I bought a lot of model T's, and even that particular car was provided with splash pans between the engine and fenders to stop debris slushing up onto the ignition wires, which was precisely the trouble with the cars that were stalled on the Queensway the other night.
I suggest safety features do not just involve seat-belts, reinforced doors and safety windows. In the wintertime in Canada you turn the car one way by looking out of the window, and the other way by looking through your rear-view mirror. They now heat rear windows with a built-in element. However, they are not designed for Canadian conditions but for Florida and California. My own car is full of junk under the hood to prevent smog in California. There are six or eight contraptions I have never seen before- and I have been doing mechanical work for a number of years. There are wires and hoses
January 29, 1970

going in all directions. Cars today do not give the better gas mileage they are supposed to, but instead cut down smog. If you want to take off the air filter and put Quickstart in the carburettor, you will find it difficult even to reach the carburettor.
We are not building cars that are safe in Canadian conditions. I suggest we should have full control over cars at all times, instead of being forced to reach down to push in a choke or to scrape snow off the windows and all the rest of it. Certainly in Ottawa the roads do not lend themselves to devoting much time to the mechanics of driving.
In Canada there has been developed a studded tire that is really useful only about three times a year, though it has done some good work. It was introduced with a great promotional drive. The department of highways now tells us that it will cost a fortune to repair the roads and they will have to crack down on studs. These studs work well when changing from summer to winter driving conditions. When we get the first two inches of snow on the roads and are not sure how to drive, studded tires are very useful.

AIR TRANSPORT-DISCONTINUANCE OF WESTERN MANITOBA SERVICE BY TRANSAIR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the minister is in the House tonight, because I want to discuss briefly a question which I posed on January 14 regarding regional air policy in western Canada. In response to the question the minister indicated that as a result of recent submissions by Transair, which is the regional carrier for the Manitoba and Saskatchewan region, he would be coming up with a solution which would be entirely satisfactory to myself and those I represent. The reason I pursue the matter tonight is that as a result of a series of discussions and negotiations the picture has changed somewhat since January 14, and certain points need clarifying.
I should like to point out to the minister, and I am sure he is aware of this, that the history of the regional policy in this part of Canada starts with a period when Air Canada provided a class 1 service. It was withdrawn, and Air Canada was replaced by Transair under subsidy. Finally, there was a removal of the subsidy and Transair was carrying on the class 1 service without subsidy.
I stress the importance of the continuance of class 1 service because there is uncertainty as to whether airport operating subsidies which apply to regional carriers and large airports used by carriers providing class 1 service, as well as subsidies for a passenger terminal building which is now under discussion, are to be tied in with the continuation of class 1 service.
As a result of discussions it has been indicated that the freight and air express business on this western lateral of the regional service has been increasing substantially during the past year or so. This is directly related to the encouraging growth of the industry in this part of the west under the incentive of the regional development program. It would seem to me that adequate air transportation is basic to a regional incentive program and would run along parallel lines.

During the discussions it became apparent that Transair has agreed to continue this class 1 service on the western lateral. The only point in doubt is whether it will continue service into the city of Brandon. Brandon is the second city in Manitoba; it has been designated as the second city for industrial growth in that province. It would be a strange anomaly if Brandon was overflown in the interests of Regina, Saskatchewan, particularly when it can be demonstrated that most of the revenue is generated between Winnipeg and Brandon, not Regina and Winnipeg.

This service is provided by four daily flights with Air Canada DC-9s. I think one can understand that when there is a choice between pure jet and turbo jet, the DC-9 service will get the business. I hope the minister-I now he is giving this matter very serious consideration-will be able to develop a policy in such a way that the revenues and losses will be equalized over the entire system.
For example, extra revenue from airmail contracts, and the possibility of an extension of this, if the eastern lateral is to go through the Lakehead to Toronto might be taken into consideration. I would suggest that an alternate service such as a seven-passenger light aircraft service would be quite inadequate to meet the industrial needs of this part of western Manitoba. Perhaps a seven-passenger service would be an excellent means by which to supplement the A-class service already in operation, and which obviously is to continue on the western lateral, so that the best connection could be made with the connecting flights out of the city of Winnipeg.
I know this would tap the substantial passenger potential out of western Manitoba which has not yet been realized, largely because Transair has been so busy surviving that it has not been able to develop an adequate market policy. The present discussion and considerations provide an opportunity to establish a regional air policy that would really work for this important developing part of Canada. I am sure under the leadership of the minister this will be achieved, and I trust the hon. gentleman will be able to give us this assurance tonight.

I should like to refer to the situation created by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Maekasey) in so far as his fine specialists are concerned. The minister says he backs the force. The following appeared in a press article:
Labour Minister Bryce Maekasey is confident his new industrial peacekeeping force of five industry specialists will not get chewed up in battles between labour and management.
For one thing, the force will be backed up by Bryce Maekasey.
At a news conference today, the Labour Minister explained that the specialists will maintain regular contacts with senior union and management officials and will be able to identify obstacles to agreement long before the two parties collide in bargaining sessions.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the President of the Treasury Board, that he should ask the Minister of Labour to assign immediately one of these specialists to the federal negotiating bargaining table, because I am certain that in the present circumstances collective bargaining will never be achieved so far as this government is concerned.
My only purpose tonight in bringing this matter forward is to try to impress upon the government its importance. According to the news release, the Minister of Labour suggested that the experience with the traditional approach to conciliation has shown that government assistance frequently came too late to prevent the development of serious disputes. In a newspaper article we find the following:

I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that if we are looking for confrontation, that is all we will get. Again I suggest that this is exactly the position in which the government finds itself today. The minister also said:

I sincerely suggest to the minister that to achieve a settlement of disputes requires negotiation. I believe there is a general feeling of appreciation for this approach, but I also suggest in all humility that the Minister of Labour assign one of his new industrial specialists to beguile the President of the Treasury Board in order that the latter may appreciate what is going on in so far as negotiations are concerned. I am sure that ultimately he will convince the President of the Treasury Board that sincere relations cannot be entered into as frivolously and as temporarily as has recently been the case. I suggest that this country cannot stand this type of collective negotiation. Either we are sincere in setting up negotiations, or we will cause a confrontation. In conclusion let me quote the Minister of Labour, who said:
To maintain contact with the principal management officials and trade union leaders in a specified industry or industries and become familiar with their organizations, policies and practices-
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the greatest mistake the Minister of Labour has made to date is that he has not assigned one specialist to ensure that there will be collective bargaining as we know it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that what I have just listened to is a request for information. The hon. member has been giving advice.

He suggests, furthermore, that we should never have collective bargaining in the public service unless officers of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) are assigned to in effect, I suppose, conduct the bargaining process. I think the hon. gentleman should know that collective bargaining in the public service is substantially by mutual agreement between bargaining agents and the Treasury Board, to be conducted in private. As a consequence, any information regarding negotiations is assumed to be speculation or rumour, and those who rely on it are allowing themselves to be misled.
This was a long and sincere collective bargaining process. It resulted in an agreement which was, I am advised, satisfactory to the penitentiary staffs and is a clear example of the success, not the failure, of the collective bargaining process. I have had relatively little experience with collective bargaining, but I do know that the party who states at the outset its final position and does not budge from that is accused, and rightly so, of inflexibility. The tactic is to start out with something considerably less than what will ultimately be offered. The representatives on the other side of the bargaining unit ask for considerably more than they hope to get.

DISTINGUISHED SERVICE AWARDS-REFERENCE OF INTERDEPARTMENTAL STUDY TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last few days a number of questions have been asked of the ministry about the matter of distinguished service awards. While the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) has been very forthright in stating, "There is no intention whatever to downgrade the awards which gallant and brave Canadians have received in the past from the sovereign", it seems clear that the minister has not been kept fully informed or taken completely into the confidence, apparently, of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) or whoever is in charge of an interdepartmental committee studying this matter.


I regret to say that it seems the Secretary of State, by his evasive answers, wishes to hide something. I would like to be assured of three things, Mr. Speaker, and I will try to be brief. One, I think, can be taken for granted but it is well it should be on record, and that is the decorations of a given grade awarded in the past will not be downgraded by any past or future award. To take an extreme example, I want to be assured that our Sergeant-at-Arms will never be requested to wear his Canadian Volunteer Service Medal ahead of his Victoria Cross.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Second, I hope that the parliamentary secretary can assure me that Commonwealth decorations, especially the ones instituted specifically for the armed forces for peacetime acts of gallantry, will continue to be awarded to the Canadian forces. I am thinking of such decorations as the Air Force Cross. It may be that since this government has done away with the Royal Canadian Air Force, it may feel that its role in life is to do away with the Air Force Cross as well and thus tidy-up the matter. Frankly, I do not see it that way. Surely, if members of the armed forces wear with pride the United Nations service ribbons, it is at least as fitting that Commonwealth awards should continue to be granted.
Third, I should like to be assured that any further Canadian orders or awards which may be instituted will be suitably integrated as to precedence with Commonwealth awards which have been or may be awarded to Canadians by the Crown on the recommendation of the Canadian government, so that it will be recognized, as it was for instance, that the Victoria Cross and the George Cross take precedence over the Order of Canada which was instituted in 1967. Furthermore, Canadians want to be assured that a bigot has not set the termites gnawing away at the framework of our nation in some dark corner of the Department of the Secretary of State,

speechtext: Hear, hear!

The traditions and practises of a nation in the matter of awards are part of the symbolism which gives its citizens a feeling of belonging to their country or to their brand of civilization. There are many traditions that members of the Commonwealth, especially the older members such as Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Great Britain, have built up together. We as a country will be poorer if we go on tearing them

down on the basis of some narrow-minded bigotry growing out of a shortsighted and provincial immaturity.
This matter, Mr. Speaker, is one on which there should be a measure of consensus, if that is at all possible. It should have the approval of Canadians generally. It should be resolved in a manner that will ensure a continuation of that approval. Therefore, I hope that before any final decision is taken by the government in this matter, the report of the committee will be studied by a standing or special committee of this House.
